# Tidy data {background-color="#4C326A"}

## The same data, many shapes

The same information can be stored in many different table layouts.

. . .

Most of them make analysis harder than it needs to be.

. . .

[Tidy data]{.highlight-peach} is one consistent layout that fits the tidyverse, so `dplyr`, `ggplot2`, and the rest all work without reshaping first.

## Data semantics

Before we can say what makes a dataset tidy, we need a shared vocabulary for what is in it. A [dataset]{.highlight-peach} is a collection of values, each one a number or a string.

. . .

Every value belongs to both a variable and an observation:

::: {.incremental}
- A [variable]{.highlight-peach} holds all the values that measure the same attribute (height, temperature, duration) across units
- An [observation]{.highlight-peach} holds all the values measured on the same unit (a person, a day, a country-year) across attributes
:::

## The three rules

::: {.incremental}
- Each [variable]{.highlight-peach} forms a column
- Each [observation]{.highlight-peach} forms a row
- Each [cell]{.highlight-peach} is a single measurement
:::

. . .

::: {.task}
If your table follows these three rules, it is tidy. Almost everything else this module does is about getting there.
:::

## Tidy in practice

`tidyr` ships with the same dataset in several shapes. This one is tidy:

```{r}
#| label: table1
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

table1
```

. . .

One row per country-year, one column per variable: `cases` and `population`.

## A messy version

The same numbers, but the values `cases` and `population` are hidden in a `type` column:

```{r}
#| label: table2
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

table2
```

. . .

Now a single observation (one country-year) is spread over [two rows]{.highlight-peach}.

## Why tidy data pays off

::: {.incremental}
- One consistent layout to learn, instead of one per dataset
- Variables live in columns, exactly where `ggplot2` and `dplyr` expect them
- Vectorized operations work naturally down each column
- Less time reshaping, more time analysing
:::

# Reshaping with tidyr {background-color="#4C326A"}

## What tidyr does

`tidyr` is the tidyverse package for [reshaping]{.highlight-peach} tables into tidy form. It is loaded with the tidyverse.

. . .

Its main jobs:

::: {.incremental}
- **Pivoting**: switching between long and wide layouts
- **Splitting and combining** columns
- **Nesting and unnesting** columns
- **Treating missing values**
:::

## Pivoting: what is it?

[Pivoting]{.highlight-peach} reshapes a table by moving information between rows and columns, without changing the data itself.

. . .

Two directions:

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Longer**

Many columns into fewer columns and more rows.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Wider**

Fewer columns into many columns and fewer rows.
:::

::::

. . .

::: {.task}
They are inverses of each other: `pivot_longer()` undoes `pivot_wider()` and vice versa.
:::

# pivot_longer() {background-color="#4C326A"}

## When to go longer

A common problem: column [names are values]{.highlight-peach}, not variables.

```{r}
#| label: table4a
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

table4a
```

. . .

`1999` and `2000` are years, not variable names. The numbers are all `cases`.

## `pivot_longer()`

```{r}
#| label: longer-basic
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

table4a |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(`1999`, `2000`),
    names_to = "year",
    values_to = "cases"
  )
```

## Reading the arguments

::: {.incremental}
- `cols`: which columns to pivot (the year columns here)
- `names_to`: name of the new column holding the [old column names]{.highlight-peach}
- `values_to`: name of the new column holding the [old cell values]{.highlight-peach}
:::

. . .

::: {.task}
The columns not listed in `cols` are kept as identifiers, repeated down the new rows.
:::

# pivot_wider() {background-color="#4C326A"}

## When to go wider

The opposite problem: one observation is spread over [several rows]{.highlight-peach}. Recall `table2`:

```{r}
#| label: table2-again
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

head(table2, 4)
```

. . .

`cases` and `population` should be two columns, not two rows.

## `pivot_wider()`

```{r}
#| label: wider-basic
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

table2 |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = type,
    values_from = count
  )
```

## Reading the arguments

::: {.incremental}
- `names_from`: the column whose values become [new column names]{.highlight-peach}
- `values_from`: the column whose values [fill the new columns]{.highlight-peach}
:::

. . .

::: {.task}
`pivot_wider()` often makes data less tidy. It is most useful for building summary tables for humans to read, not for further analysis.
:::

# More tidyr tools {background-color="#4C326A"}

## Splitting one column into many

In `table3`, `cases` and `population` are crammed into a single `rate` column:

```{r}
#| label: table3
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

table3
```

## Splitting one column into many

`separate_wider_delim()` splits a column on a [separator]{.highlight-peach}:

```{r}
#| label: separate
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

table3 |>
  separate_wider_delim(
    rate,
    delim = "/",
    names = c("cases", "population")
  )
```

## Combining several columns into one

`unite()` is the reverse, gluing columns together:

```{r}
#| label: unite
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

table5 <- table1 |>
  unite("country_year", country, year, sep = "_")

head(table5, 3)
```

## Nesting columns

`nest()` collapses a group of rows into a [single cell]{.highlight-peach} holding a small tibble:

```{r}
#| label: nest
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

nested <- table1 |>
  nest(data = c(year, cases, population))

nested
```

. . .

One row per country, with all its measurements tucked away in `data`.

. . .

::: {.task}
Nesting shines when you want to fit one model or make one plot per group, using a column of tibbles.
:::

## Unnesting columns

`unnest()` expands those cells back into ordinary rows:

```{r}
#| label: unnest
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

nested |>
  unnest(data)
```

## Treating missing values

`tidyr` has dedicated tools for `NA`:

| Function | What it does |
|----------|--------------|
| `drop_na()` | remove rows containing `NA` |
| `replace_na()` | swap `NA` for a chosen value |
| `fill()` | carry the last value down (or up) |
| `complete()` | add rows for missing combinations |

## Missing values in action

```{r}
#| label: na-tools
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

sales <- tibble(
  quarter = c("Q1", NA, NA, "Q2"),
  revenue = c(100, 150, NA, 200)
)

sales |>
  fill(quarter) |>
  replace_na(list(revenue = 0))
```

# Joining data {background-color="#4C326A"}

## Why join?

Real projects rarely keep everything in one table.

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- Measurements in one file, site descriptions in another
- Short codes in your data, with their full meanings stored in a separate lookup table
- Results you produced, joined back to the original records
:::

. . .

[Joins]{.highlight-peach} combine two tables by matching rows on a shared [key]{.highlight-peach}.

## Two small tables

`dplyr` ships two tiny tables that share a `name` column:

```{r}
#| label: bands
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

band_members
band_instruments
```

## The mutating joins

All take the form `*_join(x, y)` and add the columns of `y` to `x`. They differ in [which rows they keep]{.highlight-peach}:

| Function | Keeps |
|----------|-------|
| `inner_join()` | rows matched in **both** tables |
| `left_join()` | all rows of `x` |
| `right_join()` | all rows of `y` |
| `full_join()` | all rows of **either** table |

## Picturing the joins

![](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/diagrams/join/venn.png){fig-alt="Venn diagrams showing the difference between inner, left, right and full joins" width="70%"}

::: {.smallest}
Diagram from Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel & Grolemund, [R for Data Science (2e)](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/joins.html#fig-join-venn), licensed CC BY-NC-ND 3.0.
:::

## `left_join()`: keep everything in `x`

```{r}
#| label: left-join
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

band_members |>
  left_join(band_instruments, by = "name")
```

. . .

Mick has no instrument, so the new column is `NA`. No member is dropped.

## `inner_join()`: keep only matches

```{r}
#| label: inner-join
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

band_members |>
  inner_join(band_instruments, by = "name")
```

. . .

Only John and Paul appear in both tables, so only they survive.

## `full_join()`: keep everyone

```{r}
#| label: full-join
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

band_members |>
  full_join(band_instruments, by = "name")
```

. . .

Everyone is kept; gaps on either side become `NA`.

## The key with `by`

`by` names the column(s) used to match rows:

::: {.incremental}
- `by = "name"`: match on a shared column name
- `by = join_by(id == person_id)`: match columns with [different names]{.highlight-peach}
- omit it and `dplyr` matches on all shared names, printing a message
:::

. . .

::: {.task}
Always be explicit about the key. A silent match on the wrong columns is a hard bug to spot.
:::

## Filtering joins

Two joins use `y` only to [filter]{.highlight-peach} `x`, never adding columns:

```{r}
#| label: semi-anti
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

band_members |>
  anti_join(band_instruments, by = "name")
```

::: {.incremental}
- `semi_join()`: keep rows of `x` that **have** a match
- `anti_join()`: keep rows of `x` that have **no** match
:::

# Metadata {background-color="#4C326A"}

## What is metadata?

[Metadata]{.highlight-peach} is data about your data: the documentation that lets someone else (or future you) understand and reuse a project.

. . .

::: {.task}
A dataset without metadata is a pile of numbers. With metadata, it is evidence.
:::

## Documenting a project

Project-level documentation usually lives in a [README]{.highlight-peach} file and covers:

::: {.incremental}
- **General information**: title, author, purpose, date
- **Access information**: licence, how to cite, where it lives
- **Methodological information**: how the data were collected and processed
:::

## Documenting the data itself

For the data, you write a [data dictionary]{.highlight-peach} (also called a codebook).

. . .

It describes each variable. At a minimum:

::: {.incremental}
- the **variable name** as it appears in the file
- a plain-language **description**
:::

. . .

Often also: units, type, allowed values, and codes for missing data.

## A data dictionary as a table

| variable | description | units |
|----------|-------------|-------|
| `country` | country name | |
| `year` | year of measurement | |
| `cases` | confirmed TB cases | count |
| `population` | population that year | people |

. . .

::: {.task}
For the capstone project, save it as `dictionary.csv` in your processed data folder.
:::

# Organizing a project {background-color="#4C326A"}

## A place for everything

A predictable folder structure means anyone can find their way around:

``` {.plain}
.
├── R
│   └── 01-data-preparation.R
├── data
│   ├── processed
│   │   ├── README.md
│   │   ├── dictionary.csv
│   │   └── analysis.csv
│   └── raw
│       └── survey_05112025.xlsx
├── docs
│   ├── index.qmd
│   └── index.html
└── project.Rproj
```

## Reading the tree

::: {.incremental}
- `R/`: scripts that **do** things, mainly data preparation
- `data/raw/`: the original files, [never edited by hand]{.highlight-peach}
- `data/processed/`: clean data plus its README and dictionary
- `docs/`: the rendered report and its source
- `project.Rproj`: opens the project in RStudio
:::

## One golden rule

[Raw data is read-only.]{.highlight-peach}

. . .

You never overwrite the files in `data/raw/`. Every cleaning step reads from `raw/`, transforms in R, and writes to `processed/`.

. . .

::: {.task}
This way, the path from messy original to clean dataset is always reproducible: delete `processed/`, re-run the script, get it back.
:::

# R scripts {background-color="#4C326A"}

## Beyond Quarto

So far you have written everything in [Quarto]{.highlight-peach} (`.qmd`) files: prose, code, and output woven together.

. . .

An [R script]{.highlight-peach} (`.R`) is different: it is [pure R code]{.highlight-peach}, no YAML, no markdown, no chunks.

. . .

Comments start with `#`; everything else is code that runs top to bottom.

## What a script looks like

``` {.r}
# 01-data-preparation.R
# Clean the raw survey data

library(tidyverse)

raw <- read_csv("data/raw/survey.csv")

clean <- raw |>
  filter(!is.na(value)) |>
  mutate(date = ymd(date))

write_csv(clean, "data/processed/analysis.csv")
```

## Script or Quarto?

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**R script**

- A job to run start to finish
- Data cleaning, downloads
- No narrative needed
- Produces files, not a report
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Quarto**

- A document to read
- Analysis with explanation
- Prose, figures, tables
- Renders to HTML or PDF
:::

::::

. . .

::: {.task}
A common pattern: scripts prepare the data, Quarto reports on it.
:::

## Running a script

::: {.incremental}
- In RStudio: the **Source** button, or `Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + S`
- Line by line: `Ctrl/Cmd + Enter`, just like in a chunk
- From another file: `source("R/01-data-preparation.R")`
:::

. . .

`source()` runs the whole script, as if you had typed every line.

## Integrating scripts with Quarto

Keep the heavy lifting in a script, then [call it]{.highlight-peach} from your report:

````
```{{r}}
#| label: prepare
#| include: false

source("R/01-data-preparation.R")
```
````

. . .

The script writes `analysis.csv`; the report reads it:

````
```{{r}}
analysis <- read_csv("data/processed/analysis.csv")
```
````

## Why split the work?

::: {.incremental}
- The report stays focused on [results]{.highlight-peach}, not cleaning code
- Slow preparation runs once, not on every render
- The same clean data can feed several reports
- Each file has one clear job
:::

. . .

::: {.task}
This is exactly the structure of the capstone project: a preparation script in `R/`, a report in `docs/`.
:::
